summary: Redwood AE+SE ran an Optimize walkthrough focused on batching and prefix/KV cache strategies for Mariner Payments' customer-facing fraud detection pipeline. Main outcomes: measured latency vs cost tradeoffs, recommended KV cache footprint, suggested initial pilot configuration and next steps to run a 2-week pilot with dedicated pooling and targeted benchmarks.
transcript:
00:00 Avery Chen: Alright hi everyone thanks for joining, we'll kick off in a sec, hey Maya?
00:07 Maya Gupta: hey, hi thanks, excited to see the optimize walk through, we've been looking at token costs on our auth flow.
00:12 Avery Chen: sweet, so agenda, quick context, dylan will run through batching and kv cache recommendations, then cost model, then q&a, and next steps. should be about 45 minutes plus q&a.
00:28 Dylan Park: cool, I'll share screen — um quick note, some folks we've seen say "kv cache" and "prefix cache" interchangeably so i'll call out both.
00:36 Owen Lee: thanks, and just to flag, our main goal is to hit sub-150ms p95 on auth path and keep cost per 1M requests under $200 - ish.
00:48 Dylan Park: got it. quick qual - what's your current call pattern? how many tokens per session, average sequence length?
00:55 Sara Kim: most auth checks are light, like 60-120 tokens, but the fraud step where we do context+history is longer, often 800-1k tokens.
01:07 Dylan Park: ok that split matters a lot for batching and kv cache hit rates.
01:15 Avery Chen: also who owns infra - Luis?
01:18 Luis Ramirez: yep infra, we run a mix of GKE and some VPC peered dbs, we prefer VPC peering for private deployment but open to dedicated.
01:26 Dylan Park: perfect. i'm going to start with batching fundamentals - continuous batching vs fixed-window batching.
01:34 Dylan Park: (screen) so continuous batching gives lower latency for small spikes because the runtime builds batches up to a configurable max in a short horizon, whereas fixed-window is simpler but can add wait.
01:46 Maya Gupta: is this where batching hurts p95? we saw some weird latency spikes.
01:50 Dylan Park: yes, if you set the max_batch_size too large and sequence length is variable you can end up blocking on long sequences. recommended pattern: separate routes by expected sequence length and set per-route max batch and max_wait_ms.
02:06 Rina Patel: for your auth path, set small max_batch_size (like 8-16) and max_wait 20-30ms; for fraud step use larger batch sizes and looser waits.
02:16 Owen Lee: that makes sense, how does the cost change?
02:19 Dylan Park: here's where our cost model comes in. two levers: throughput efficiency via batching (more tokens per GPU per second) and cache hit rate via KV/prefix cache which reduces total tokens sent to model.
02:31 Dylan Park: example numbers - unoptimized: 1M requests, avg tokens per request 400 -> 400M tokens processed. with batching improvements we might get 1.8x token throughput improvement (effectively lower per-token infra cost). with kv cache hitting 30% you reduce token count to 280M tokens.
02:49 Sara Kim: our current observed token/call for fraud is pretty high because we re-send context. can you explain prefix cache vs kv cache again?
02:58 Dylan Park: sure. prefix cache stores repeated leading tokens across calls (like system prompt + user profile), kv cache stores key-value attention caches per session allowing continuation without re-sending all previous tokens. prefix cache helps if you have repeated prompt scaffolding; kv cache helps large contexts and multi-turn flows.
03:17 Maya Gupta: are both available on hosted? any extra security implications?
03:21 Avery Chen: yes both supported across hosted and dedicated; for private we can keep the control plane separate. security: KV caches can be encrypted at rest and you can use KMS/HSM integrations for key management - dylan will drop the link to our security docs.
03:37 Dylan Park: (note) link: https://redwood.ai/security - will share in follow up. also for VPC private deployments we have options for customer-managed VPC peering.
03:46 Luis Ramirez: good. question - how big are kv cache objects typically in RAM? we're worried about footprint.
03:51 Dylan Park: good question. size scales with model and cache length. ballpark: for an Llama- or Mistral-class 33B-ish model, per-session kv cache for 1k tokens is ~12-18MB. so 100k active sessions -> ~1.2-1.8TB. for shorter sessions it's much smaller.
04:13 Owen Lee: ok that's useful. so we need to estimate active sessions for pilot.
04:17 Sara Kim: we have about 15k daily active users but only ~2k sessions hitting fraud logic per day currently.
04:24 Dylan Park: great, so pilot footprint will be modest. next i want to show a quick tradeoff chart - latency vs cost as we vary batch size and cache hit rate.
04:33 Dylan Park: (screen) example: p95 latency baseline 180ms without batching and 0% cache. with small batch (8) and 30% cache we hit 120ms p95 and cost reduces ~25%. with larger batch (64) p95 can regress on short routes.
04:53 Maya Gupta: can we do hybrid routing - like route auth to small-batch low-latency nodes and route fraud to high-batch nodes?
04:58 Dylan Park: absolutely - smart routing by route is a core feature. you can pin a model variant and routing policy per route and have fallbacks.
05:06 Rina Patel: also we recommend autoscale with burst capacity to handle spikes and avoid cold-start latency.
05:11 Luis Ramirez: how do you measure effective cost - is it tokens only or gpu time?
05:15 Dylan Park: our unit economics combines both: tokens processed, GPU time, and instance amortization for dedicated. the spreadsheet i'll share breaks down per-token cost, per-request CPU overhead, and amortized instance cost.
05:27 Avery Chen: we prepared a tailored cost model for mariner based on your sample distribution - i'll walk through the key rows.
05:33 Avery Chen: (screen) sheet: three scenarios - conservative, realistic, aggressive. conservative assumes 10% cache hit, small batching; realistic 30% cache hit + route separation; aggressive 60% cache hit plus quantization on model.
05:48 Maya Gupta: quantization? we need to be careful about quality.
05:51 Dylan Park: yes, quantization can change output slightly; we recommend A/B evals on your prompt set. Optimize has eval hooks to track quality regressions per prompt set.
06:02 Sara Kim: do you have samples for our fraud prompts? we can run quick eval.
06:06 Avery Chen: please send sample prompt set (Sara) - we'll plug into eval harness during pilot.
06:11 Dylan Park: in the spreadsheet the realistic scenario reduced token cost by ~35% compared to baseline. combined with dedicated reserved instance amortization you can get another 20% reduction at scale.
06:24 Owen Lee: that seems promising. one more question on cache TTL - how long to keep kv caches live?
06:29 Dylan Park: depends - for session-based flows set TTL to session length plus slack, for long-term user context use prefix cache with explicit invalidation and smaller key size. TTL choice impacts RAM footprint and hit rate.
06:41 Luis Ramirez: for compliance we need audit logs for cache hits/errors - does Redwood expose that?
06:45 Rina Patel: yes, console exposes per-route metrics, token breakdown, and audit logs. we can push logs to your SIEM or S3.
06:54 Maya Gupta: any gotchas with multi-region? we serve users in NA/EU and need EU data residency.
06:59 Dylan Park: you can route EU traffic to EU-only nodes and pin model variants; for private deployments we support region-specific private control planes.
07:08 Jordan Price: curious about fallbacks - if dedicated pool full, do you overflow to hosted?
07:13 Avery Chen: you can configure automatic fallback to compatible model variants in hosted capacity to avoid request failures.
07:19 Maya Gupta: ok let's talk pilot - what does a 2-week pilot look like?
07:23 Avery Chen: pilot plan: week 0 prepare config and sample prompts, week 1 run traffic with metrics collection (latency, cost, cache hit rate, quality evals), week 2 tuning and final report. we can run this on a small dedicated pool or on hosted with routing rules.
07:40 Dylan Park: recommend starting hosted dedicated pool (small) so we can iterate quickly then move to dedicated if performance/stability good.
07:47 Luis Ramirez: pricing for dedicated - is it monthly commit?
07:50 Avery Chen: we can do a short-term reserved for pilot, then convert to a monthly commit for production. pricing sheet will be included.
07:59 Maya Gupta: any specific logs we should collect from our side?
08:03 Sara Kim: we'll export sample prompts and request traces (anonymized) and provide p95 targets.
08:09 Dylan Park: perfect. i'll also ask engineering for a short benchmark harness to run locally if you want to emulate peak traffic.
08:16 Owen Lee: about 3rd party models - we might need to evaluate Mistral vs other models - are both available?
08:21 Dylan Park: yes we have curated open models and verified performance profiles; we recommend trying the 13B- or 33B-class for your latency/cost needs.
08:31 Maya Gupta: can Redwood help with SSO and RBAC onboarding?
08:34 Rina Patel: yes we support SAML/SSO, SCIM provisioning, RBAC, and per-route ACLs. we'll share our onboarding checklist.
08:44 Dylan Park: back to caching - one more concrete recommendation: for auth route use prefix cache for system prompt and small ephemeral user signals; for fraud route enable kv cache with session affinity and aggressive eviction policy tuned to session activity.
08:58 Sara Kim: how do we measure hit rate in the console?
09:02 Rina Patel: console shows per-route cache hit rate, token saved per time window, and cost delta. we'll give you a demo view.
09:10 Avery Chen: ok i'm going to go over the tailored numbers in the sheet quickly -
09:13 Avery Chen: conservative scenario monthlyized cost: $3,200 for model infra + $1,000 request overhead - realistic: $2,400 infra + $700 overhead after batching+cache; aggressive: $1,800 infra with quantization and high cache. these are rough.
09:34 Maya Gupta: those order-of-magnitude savings look compelling.
09:37 Luis Ramirez: what about SLA - p95, uptime?
09:40 Avery Chen: Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency targets; hosted has best-effort but we offer SLA add-ons for enterprise. we'll attach SLA doc.
09:49 Jordan Price: can you highlight any risks?
09:52 Dylan Park: main risks: cache miss patterns driving cold requests, quality drift from quantization, and orchestration complexity if you try to tune too many knobs at once. mitigations: start narrow, run evals, iterative tuning.
10:05 Maya Gupta: great. now open q&a - Sara: are there examples of other payments customers?
10:10 Avery Chen: yes we have case studies - mariner is in early convo but we worked with Aurora Finance on similar flows, i'll include references.
10:17 Owen Lee: ok final checklist - socialize cost numbers with finance and security review with our compliance team.
10:23 Avery Chen: cool. recap and next steps: we'll send the spreadsheet, security docs, and a pilot proposal; Sara will send prompts; Dylan will share network notes.
10:34 Maya Gupta: sounds good, thanks all.
10:38 Avery Chen: thanks everyone - we'll follow up in email and put items into the CRM.
10:42 (call ends)
